metadata.document: SUBMISSION ON THE RESOURCE MANAGEMENT REFORM BILL

cleaned_body_text: The Environmental Defence Society (EDS) is a public interest environmental law group, formed in 1971. It has a membership that consists largely of resource management professionals. The focus of EDS’s work is on achieving good environmental outcomes through improving the quality of New Zealand’s legal and policy frameworks and statutory decision-making processes. EDS welcomes the opportunity to comment on the Resource Management Reform Bill which amends the Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA), Local Government (Auckland Transitional Provisions) Act 2010 (LGATPA), and the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act 1987. This submission addresses amendments to section 76 of the RMA, amendments to section 32 of the RMA, and amendments to the LGATPA. EDS strongly opposes the proposed restrictions on district plan rules relating to tree protection. Trees are important for a number of reasons, providing ecosystem services such as habitat for biodiversity, improved water quality, reduced storm water run-off, reduced erosion, and carbon absorption, alongside amenity and cultural values. In urban environments, trees are an integral part of maintaining liveable cities, especially where intensification is occurring. The retention of trees is essential to meet the sustainable management purpose of the RMA under section 5(2), matters of national importance under section 6, territorial authority functions under section 31, and the New Zealand Coastal Policy Statement 2010. Furthermore, local authorities will be unable to perform functions required by the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act 2000 and the Waitakere Ranges Heritage Area Act 2008 if the proposed amendments are enacted. EDS considers the proposals flawed because the benefits of retaining trees are significant, and the amendments would require councils to invest considerable time and expense identifying individual properties, creating a complex and costly bureaucratic obligation. Instead, the RMA already contains section 32 as a mechanism to evaluate the costs and benefits of rules. EDS has developed a compromise solution which distinguishes between trimming and removal of trees, addresses trees in poor health, focuses on specific groupings of trees that achieve key benefits, and proposes precise identification methods using aerial photographs or GPS coordinates while preventing resource consent application fees for such rules. Regarding section 32 amendments, EDS supports improvements to report quality but opposes amendments drawing particular attention to opportunity costs for economic growth and employment as they risk resulting in unbalanced evaluation reports. For the LGATPA and the Auckland Unitary Plan streamlined plan-making process, EDS raises concerns regarding regulation-making powers, setting aside established RMA provisions, restrictions on council expert attendance at expert conferences, cross-examination rules, panel member quorum, recommendation scope, panel appointment by central government ministers rather than Auckland Council, lack of requirement for an Environment Court judge, and the restriction to a single hearing panel. EDS concludes that proposed amendments to section 76 should be rejected or the alternative compromise accepted, and that proposed amendments to section 32 and the Auckland Unitary Plan process must be revised to address the concerns raised.
